article.title: Mass Deportation Disaster
article.author: Joe Mathews
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. To clean up the disaster of mass deportation, the United States will eventually need more than an amnesty. It will need two amnesties. One for the millions of victims of the cruel, violent, and flagrantly unlawful deportation campaign tearing through American communities. And another for those who took part in making the deportations happen. The Trump administration is deporting people without due process, including to faraway continents and unfamiliar countries. Many of those removed were legal immigrants who followed the rules and obtained visas or work authorization—and got kicked out anyway. Families have been shattered, human rights cancelled, local economies damaged, and whole segments of society forced into hiding. Related: How the University of California Became Both a Gateway and a Gatekeeper When this nightmare finally ends, California and the United States will face a monumental challenge: How do we reunite families, uncover the full scale of what was done in our name, compensate victims, restore the rule of law, and hold official perpetrators accountable? The solution is what I am calling the Double Amnesty. The first amnesty is straightforward: a comprehensive, unencumbered program granting permanent residency, and creating a speedy process for obtaining citizenship for everyone caught in the U.S. regime’s anti-immigrant pogrom. This first amnesty starts with allowing readmission for deported people, with priority going to immigrants the Trump administration sent to third-party countries. Restitution must apply universally—to undocumented immigrants, long-term legal residents, migrants with temporary status, and U.S. citizens mistaken for migrants. The amnesty must also cover citizens and residents who were punished or injured for defending their neighbors against deportation. They are heroes, not criminals. This is the only practical way to return millions of human beings to the light, stabilize our economy, and shrink the unauthorized population. The 1986 amnesty law championed by President Reagan legalized nearly 3 million people—and, eventually, many of their family members. It also reduced unauthorized immigration to the country . Immigration restrictionists claim that relentless enforcement deters unauthorized presence. In reality, the opposite is true . When people are arrested in immigration courts or naturalization appointments, the message is: Stay undocumented, stay in the shadows. The current administration has manufactured more undocumented immigration, not reduced it. By stripping legal status en masse — revoking Temporary Protected Status (TPS) , ending protection for Dreamers , rescinding humanitarian parole , and ripping away valid visas —the government deliberately and illegally created more than 1 million so-called “illegal” immigrants. Related: California’s Climate Law Still Matters Globally Which brings me to the second amnesty of the Double Amnesty—in which the U.S. would offer administrative and legal relief to the government employees, ICE agents, CBP officers, and bureaucrats who participated in executing this campaign. This amnesty may be harder to swallow. Many of us would prefer to prosecute law enforcement officials who broke the law and hurt immigrants, but the scale of the lawless deportation campaign makes mass prosecutions impractical. But the second amnesty does not offer forgiveness automatically. This amnesty must be strictly contingent on first establishing personal and institutional accountability, and on exposing violations. The Trump deportation machine operates in the dark, with masked law enforcement personnel, secret deportations to third countries, concealed detainee facilities, and undisclosed transfers of migrants between centers and prisons to keep them from being found by families and lawyers. As a result, deportations have been executed with staggering incompetence, shielded by bureaucratic deception, and deliberately hidden from federal courts, defense lawyers, and the public . We still do not know the true number of missing children, falsified records, or unconstitutional orders carried out in field offices across the country. To earn this second amnesty, agents and officials must go through a process of mandatory truth-telling. They must step forward and disclose every secret directive and unwritten quota, every illegal detention and unconstitutional maneuver, and every document or record withheld from courts, defense counsel, and the public. Related: Dear America: You Don't Really Know Gavin Newsom In addition, the top executives of private companies that knew of the immigration abuses and personally profited must report their activities—and forfeit every dollar they made, for their business and personally—to a restitution fund for the campaign’s victims. Once perpetrators provide full, verifiable documentation of their actions, they should receive immunity. If they lie, destroy evidence, or refuse to disclose, they must face full criminal prosecution. There is one non-negotiable exception to the amnesty: No mercy at the top. Zocalo Market Square
